'''Jeremy Shu-How Lin''' ({{Lang-zh|t=林書豪}}; born August 23, 1988) is an American former professional basketball player. He unexpectedly led a winning turnaround with the [[New York Knicks]] of the [[National Basketball Association]] (NBA) during the [[2011–12 NBA season|2011–12 season]], sparking a cultural phenomenon known as "'''Linsanity'''". <!--***The sentence is the result of extensive discussion. Please do not modify it without proposing the change on the talk page***-->Lin is the first American of Chinese or Taiwanese descent to play in the NBA, and is one of the few Asian Americans to have played in the league.<!--***The sentence is the result of extensive discussion. Please do not modify it without proposing the change on the talk page***--> He is also the first Asian American player to win an [[NBA championship]], having done so with the [[Toronto Raptors]] in [[2019 NBA Finals|2019]].

Born to a [[Taiwanese American]] family, Lin grew up in the [[San Francisco Bay Area]] and earned honors as a [[Senior (education)#High school|senior]] in high school. After receiving no [[athletic scholarship]] offers, he attended [[Harvard Crimson men's basketball|Harvard University]], where he was a three-time all-conference player in the [[Ivy League]]. [[List of National Basketball Association undrafted players|Undrafted]] out of college, Lin signed with his hometown [[Golden State Warriors]] in 2010. He seldom played in his [[rookie]] season and received [[assignment (NBA D-League)|assignments]] to the NBA Development League (now [[NBA G League]]). In 2011, Lin was [[waivers (NBA)|waived]] by both the Warriors and the [[Houston Rockets]] before joining the New York Knicks early in [[2011–12 NBA season|2011–12]].

At first, Lin played sparingly for the Knicks, and he again spent time in the development league. In February 2012, however, he was promoted to the [[starting lineup]] and led the team on a seven-game winning streak. Lin's stellar play during the season helped the Knicks make the [[2012 NBA playoffs|2012 playoffs]]; it also catapulted him to international fame. Lin appeared on the covers of ''[[Sports Illustrated]]'' and ''[[Time (magazine)|Time]]'' and was named to the [[Time 100|''Time'' 100]] as one of the most influential people in the world. In July 2012, Lin won the [[ESPY Award]] for [[Best Breakthrough Athlete ESPY Award|Breakthrough Athlete of the Year]].

Following his Knicks tenure, Lin played for the Houston Rockets, [[Los Angeles Lakers]], [[Charlotte Hornets]], [[Brooklyn Nets]], [[Atlanta Hawks]], and [[Toronto Raptors]]. While he experienced some success in Houston and Charlotte, he battled injuries in the ensuing seasons. In August 2019, he left the NBA and signed with the [[Beijing Ducks]], where he became an [[All-Star]] in the [[Chinese Basketball Association]] (CBA). Attempting to return to the NBA, Lin played with the Warriors' development team in 2021. He returned to the CBA and played with the Ducks and later the [[Guangzhou Loong Lions]]. He left the Loong Lions midseason in [[2022–23 Chinese Basketball Association season|2022–23]] and joined [[Kaohsiung 17LIVE Steelers]] of the [[P. League+]] (PLG) in 2023. Lin would lead the PLG in assists that season. He signed with the [[New Taipei Kings]] in 2023, winning the PLG championship in [[2024 PLG finals|2024]] and the [[Taiwan Professional Basketball League]] (TPBL) championship in [[2025 TPBL finals|2025]].

A Harvard coach remembered Lin in his freshman season as "the [physically] weakest guy on the team",<ref name="beck20120225">{{cite news |url=http://www.nytimes.com/2012/02/25/sports/basketball/the-evolution-of-jeremy-lin-as-a-point-guard.html?_r=2&pagewanted=all |title=The evolution of a point guard |work=The New York Times |date=February 25, 2012 |access-date=February 26, 2012 |author=Beck, Howard |page=D1 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120304055054/http://www.nytimes.com/2012/02/25/sports/basketball/the-evolution-of-jeremy-lin-as-a-point-guard.html?_r=2&pagewanted=all |archive-date=March 4, 2012 |url-status=dead }}</ref> but in his sophomore season (2007–08), Lin averaged 12.6 points and was named to the All-Ivy League Second Team.<ref name=Harvard/> By his junior year during the [[2008–09 NCAA Division I men's basketball season|2008–09 season]], he was the only [[NCAA Division I]] men's [[college basketball|basketball]] player ranked in the top ten in his conference for scoring (17.8), [[rebound (basketball)|rebounding]] (5.5), [[assist (basketball)|assists]] (4.3), [[steal (basketball)|steals]] (2.4), [[blocked shot]]s (0.6), [[field goal percentage]] (0.502), [[free throw]] percentage (0.744), and [[three-point shot]] percentage (0.400),<ref name=ONeil/> and was a consensus selection for the All-Ivy League First Team. ==Racial issues==
{{see also|Stereotypes of East Asians in the United States#Physicality and sports}}

During his basketball career, Lin encountered racial slurs relating to his Asian ancestry. In the sixth grade, he faced racist comments when he started playing more competitive basketball and journeying outside the Bay Area.<ref>{{cite news|first=Patrick|last=Blennerhassett|title=Jeremy Lin details racism he experienced in childhood as he opens up about mental health struggles during 'Linsanity' period|date=March 19, 2021|newspaper=South China Morning Post|url=https://www.scmp.com/sport/basketball/article/3126086/jeremy-lin-details-racism-he-experienced-childhood-he-opens-about|access-date=March 25, 2021}}</ref> While playing for Harvard, he regularly heard bigoted jeers such as "[[Wonton]] soup", "[[Sweet and sour pork]]", "Open your eyes!", "Go back to China", "Orchestra is on the other side of campus", or pseudo-Chinese gibberish.<ref name=harvard_school/><ref name=harvards_hoops/><ref name=asian_american/> According to Harvard teammate Oliver McNally, a fellow Ivy League player once called Lin the ethnic slur "[[chink]]".<ref name=harvards_hoops/>

On February 10, 2012, in the middle of a Knicks-Lakers game in which Lin scored 38 points, [[Fox Sports]] columnist [[Jason Whitlock]] posted the following on Twitter regarding Lin's sexual prowess: "Some lucky lady in NYC is gonna feel a couple inches of pain tonight".<ref>{{cite news|title=Sunday's NBA notebook: Rajon Rondo's triple-double carries Celtics over Bulls |date=February 12, 2012 |newspaper=The Detroit News |agency=Associated Press |url=http://www.detroitnews.com/article/20120212/SPORTS0102/202120342/1361/Sunday-s-NBA-notebook--Rajon-Rondo-s-triple-double-carries-Celtics-over-Bulls |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120213222359/http://www.detroitnews.com/article/20120212/SPORTS0102/202120342/1361/Sunday-s-NBA-notebook--Rajon-Rondo-s-triple-double-carries-Celtics-over-Bulls |archive-date=February 13, 2012 |url-status=dead }}</ref> ''[[Hyphen (magazine)|Hyphen]]'' wrote that Whitlock had "reinforced the insipid and insidious 'small Asian penis' stereotype".<ref>{{cite news|last=Kim |first=Sylvie |title=Spike, Jeremy, and Stopping "Asian Profi'Lin" |date=February 13, 2012 |magazine=Hyphen |url=http://www.hyphenmagazine.com/blog/archive/2012/02/spike-jeremy-and-stopping-asian-profilin |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120217025058/http://www.hyphenmagazine.com/blog/archive/2012/02/spike-jeremy-and-stopping-asian-profilin |archive-date=February 17, 2012 |url-status=dead }}</ref> The [[Asian American Journalists Association]] demanded an apology. "I debased a feel-good sports moment. For that, I'm truly sorry," apologized Whitlock.<ref>{{cite news|last=Schilken |first=Chuck |title=Fox Sports' Jason Whitlock apologizes for Jeremy Lin tweet |date=February 13, 2012 |newspaper=Los Angeles Times |url=http://latimesblogs.latimes.com/sports_blog/2012/02/fox-sports-jason-whitlock-apologizes-for-jeremy-lin-tweet.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120215070317/http://latimesblogs.latimes.com/sports_blog/2012/02/fox-sports-jason-whitlock-apologizes-for-jeremy-lin-tweet.html |archive-date=February 15, 2012 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last=Dwyer |first=Kelly |title=Jason Whitlock apologizes for his unfunny Jeremy Lin comment on Twitter |date=February 13, 2012 |publisher=Yahoo |url=https://sports.yahoo.com/blogs/nba-ball-dont-lie/jason-whitlock-apologizes-unfunny-jeremy-lin-twitter-145934497.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120213191334/http://sports.yahoo.com/blogs/nba-ball-dont-lie/jason-whitlock-apologizes-unfunny-jeremy-lin-twitter-145934497.html |archive-date=February 13, 2012 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Also in February 2012, boxer [[Floyd Mayweather Jr.]] wrote on his Twitter page, "Jeremy Lin is a good player but all the hype is because he's Asian. Lin's experience in the NBA draft was used as an example in the nonfiction psychology book ''[[The Undoing Project]]'' by Michael Lewis, which details how stereotypes can overwhelmingly influence a person's decision making, even in the face of contradictory evidence. ''The Undoing Project: A Friendship That Changed Our Minds''. p. 19.</ref> A year after the Rockets failed to draft Lin, they began to measure the speed of a player's first two steps; Lin had the quickest first move of any player measured, and he was able to change direction far more quickly than most NBA players. ==Public image and impact==
[[File:Jeremy Lin 2012 Shankbone.JPG|thumb|upright|Lin was named to the [[Time 100|''Time'' 100]] in 2012.]]

==Philanthropy==
In October 2016, Lin donated $1 million to [[Harvard University]] to support undergraduate financial aid and renovations to [[Lavietes Pavilion]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://news.harvard.edu/gazette/story/2016/10/gift-from-jeremy-lin-10-funds-financial-aid-and-lavietes-pavilion-renovation/|title=Gift from Jeremy Lin '10 funds financial aid and Lavietes Pavilion renovation|date=October 26, 2016|website=harvard.edu}}</ref>

In February 2020, Lin donated ¥1 million (about $144,370) to help those affected by the [[COVID-19 pandemic]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.scmp.com/sport/china/article/3049735/david-beckham-sun-yang-and-jeremy-lin-among-stars-supporting-wuhan|title=David Beckham, Sun Yang and Jeremy Lin among stars supporting Wuhan virus fight|work=South China Morning Post|date=February 10, 2020}}</ref> He also spoke out against the [[Xenophobia and racism related to the COVID-19 pandemic|racism related to the outbreak]], stating: "I've lived in China this past season and now being back on US soil, I'm saddened by the racist comments regarding the virus in China. There are real people suffering and real heroes working around the clock in service to others — please don't let your fear or ignorance rob you of seeing that. This world needs more compassion and empathy."<ref>{{Cite web |last=Jonathan White |date=2020-12-25 |title=Jeremy Lin's 2020: Covid-19, Donald Trump and an NBA dream |url=https://www.scmp.com/sport/china/article/3115009/jeremy-lins-2020-covid-19-donald-trump-and-nba-dream |url-status=live |archive-url=https://archive.today/20240412043606/https://www.scmp.com/sport/china/article/3115009/jeremy-lins-2020-covid-19-donald-trump-and-nba-dream |archive-date=2024-04-12 |website=[[South China Morning Post]] |language=en |quote="I've lived in China this past season and now being back on US soil, I'm saddened by the racist comments regarding the virus in China. There are real people suffering and real heroes working around the clock in service to others – please don't let your fear or ignorance rob you of seeing that," he wrote on Instagram in February. "This world needs more compassion and empathy." [...] He pledged US$300,000 to that fight as he urged his fans to contribute, while his charitable foundation in China gave 1 million yuan to the frontline in Wuhan.}}</ref><ref name=inquisitr/>

In April 2020, Lin donated $500,000 to the nonprofits [[Direct Relief]] and [[Feeding America]] to help those affected by the COVID-19 pandemic;<ref>{{cite web |date=April 13, 2020 |title=Jeremy Lin pledges up to $1 million to fight coronavirus |url=https://clutchpoints.com/nba-news-jeremy-lin-pledges-up-to-1-million-fight-coronavirus/ |work=[[ClutchPoints]]}}</ref> he also wrote an article for ''[[The Players' Tribune]]'' in which he pledged to match donations up to an additional $500,000 and encouraged unity, writing: "Again, at a time like this that requires ''everyone'' uniting to survive, COVID-19 shouldn't be about [[East vs. West]], politics, race or anything other than helping as many people as we can survive."<ref>{{cite web |last=Lin |first=Jeremy |date=April 13, 2020 |title=The Darkness Has Not Overcome It |url=https://www.theplayerstribune.com/articles/jeremy-lin-darkness-has-not-overcome-it |work=[[The Players' Tribune]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Jonathan White |date=2020-04-14 |title=Coronavirus: Jeremy Lin launches US$1 million charity campaign and urges fans to 'choose light' |url=https://www.scmp.com/sport/china/article/3079771/coronavirus-jeremy-lin-launches-us1-million-charity-campaign-and-urges |url-status=live |archive-url=https://archive.today/20240412070001/https://www.scmp.com/sport/china/article/3079771/coronavirus-jeremy-lin-launches-us1-million-charity-campaign-and-urges |archive-date=2024-04-12 |website=South China Morning Post |language=en}}</ref>

In an NBA Together Virtual Roundtable held in May 2020, Lin further spoke out against anti-Asian racism, stating: "All it would take is 10 seconds to put yourself in the position of someone who is dealing with racism or somebody who is legitimately contemplating whether to go to the grocery store to get food for themselves or to not because they're afraid of being attacked. ... Sometimes the best thing you can do is to not post the hateful comment, or don't be a troll, or take a second to think about what you're saying or doing or if you know someone acting ignorant call them out. All these things are small steps in the right direction."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://people.com/sports/jeremy-lin-addresses-anti-asian-sentiment-in-u-s-amid-covid-19-pandemic/|title=Jeremy Lin Addresses Anti-Asian Racism in U.S. amid Coronavirus Pandemic, Encourages Unity|work=People|date=May 13, 2020}}</ref>

==Personal life==
[[File:President Ma meets Jeremy Lin.jpg|thumb|left|Lin meets Taiwanese president [[Ma Ying-jeou]], 2010]]
Mostly private about his personal life, Lin announced on social media in January 2023 that he and his wife got married about two years before.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Jeremy Lin reveals he got married 'over a couple years ago' |url=https://www.nbcnews.com/news/asian-america/jeremy-lin-reveals-marriage-2-years-rcna66536 |access-date=2023-01-21 |website=NBC News |date=January 19, 2023 |language=en}}</ref> She is of Filipino descent.<ref>{{cite news |author1=陳筱琳 |author2=陳怡誠 |title=林書豪賽後透露 老婆是菲律賓人 |url=https://www.chinatimes.com/realtimenews/20231129005955-260403 |accessdate=2023-11-29 |publisher=中時新聞網 |date=2023-11-29 |quote=他回應: 「菲律賓歌手AJ Rafael是我好朋友, 我穿的是他的衣服品牌.我也覺得應該可以宣傳一下我老婆是菲律賓人, (之後到馬尼拉比賽)當然對我來說是非常有意義的一件事.」|language=Chinese}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |author=Chao Yen-hsiang |title=Jeremy Lin shares connection with Philippines following EASL win |url=https://focustaiwan.tw/sports/202311300014 |access-date=2023-12-03 |work=Focus Taiwan |date=2023-11-30 |quote=Asked about his shirt, Lin said it was a product of a brand founded by his good friend AJ Rafael, a Filipino-American singer-songwriter."Also, I think I can share this with you today, my wife is a Filipino, so for me this is very meaningful."}}</ref> His older brother, Joshua, studied dentistry at [[New York University]].<ref>{{cite news|last=Back|first=Howard|title=From Ivy Halls to the Garden, Surprise Star Jolts the N.B.A.|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2012/02/08/sports/basketball/jeremy-lin-has-burst-from-nba-novelty-act-to-knicks-star.html|newspaper=The New York Times|date=February 8, 2012|access-date=February 13, 2012}}</ref>

Lin is an [[evangelical]] Protestant, and was a leader in [[Harvard University|Harvard]]'s Asian American Christian Fellowship during his time there.<ref name="InterVarsity">[http://www.intervarsity.org/studentsoul/item/jeremy-lin Jeremy Lin: Taking Harvard Basketball to New Levels] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100322223905/http://www.intervarsity.org/studentsoul/item/jeremy-lin |date=March 22, 2010 }}, [[InterVarsity Christian Fellowship|InterVarsity.org]], Published March 12, 2010; accessed February 15, 2012.</ref><ref name="Luo">Michael Luo, [https://www.nytimes.com/2012/02/12/sports/basketball/the-knicks-jeremy-lin-faith-pride-and-points.html Lin's Appeal: Faith, Pride, and Points], ''[[The New York Times]]'', February 12, 2012, accessed February 15, 2012.</ref> He credited his NBA success to playing without pressure. "I've surrendered that to God. I'm not in a battle with what everybody else thinks anymore," said Lin.<ref name=thompson_02132012>{{cite news|author=Thompson II, Marcus |title=Exclusive: Jeremy Lin says 'Lin-sanity' was triggered by a leap of faith |date=February 13, 2012 |newspaper=San Jose Mercury News |url=http://www.mercurynews.com/jeremy-lin/ci_19954877 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120216010602/http://www.mercurynews.com/jeremy-lin/ci_19954877 |archive-date=February 16, 2012 |url-status=dead }}</ref> He hopes to become a pastor who can head up non-profit organizations, either home or abroad,<ref name=hughes>{{cite news|last=Hughes|first=Frank|title=Former Harvard standout Lin ready to prove himself with Warriors|publisher=SI.com|date=July 26, 2010|url=http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/2010/writers/frank_hughes/07/26/jeremy.lin.warriors/index.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100727043722/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/2010/writers/frank_hughes/07/26/jeremy.lin.warriors/index.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=July 27, 2010|access-date=October 23, 2010|quote=You do not hear too many NBA players talk like this, seeds of self-doubt occasionally sprouting. You also rarely hear this sentence: 'I compare myself to [Suns backup point guard] Goran Dragic.'}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nbadraft.net/jeremy-lin-interview|title=Jeremy Lin Interview|publisher=NBADraft.net|date=June 16, 2010|access-date=October 23, 2010|quote=I would be a pastor. It is something I think about doing when my playing days are over.}}</ref> and has talked of working in inner-city communities to help with underprivileged children.<ref name=lin>{{cite interview|last=Lin|first=Jeremy|interviewer=Michel Martin|title=Tell Me More|url=https://www.npr.org/templates/story/story.php?storyId=123368990|work=[[National Public Radio]]|date=February 4, 2010|access-date=October 25, 2010|quote=I mean, I get Asian jokes and, you know, when other fans try to heckle us, I don't really hear from other players very much.}}</ref>

Lin said that he understands [[Standard Chinese|Mandarin]], though he could use some help speaking it; he can also read and write a little. He took a few Mandarin classes while attending Harvard to try to improve.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nbadraft.net/jeremy-lin-interview|title=Jeremy Lin Interview|publisher=NBADraft.net|date=June 16, 2010|access-date=March 8, 2011}}</ref> After joining the Knicks in 2012, Lin slept on a couch in his brother's one-bedroom apartment on the [[Lower East Side]] of [[Manhattan]], New York City.<ref>{{cite news |url= https://www.nytimes.com/2012/02/08/sports/basketball/jeremy-lin-has-burst-from-nba-novelty-act-to-knicks-star.html|title=From Ivy Halls to the Garden, Surprise Star Jolts the N.B.A.|author=Howard Beck|newspaper=The New York Times|date=February 8, 2012|access-date =February 16, 2012}}</ref> He moved to a luxury condo in [[White Plains, New York]], after his Knicks contract became guaranteed.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/jeremy-lin-moves-from-couch-to-condo/ |date= February 15, 2012|title=Jeremy Lin moves from couch to condo |author= Bailey Johnson|publisher=CBS News|access-date =February 16, 2012}}</ref>

Lin is a fan of the video game ''[[Dota 2]]'', having played the first game in the series, ''[[Defense of the Ancients]]'', since his second year of high school. He appeared in ''[[Free to Play (film)|Free to Play]]'', the 2014 documentary centered around the game, in which he described ''Dota 2'' as a "way of life" that helped him better connect with his family and friends.<ref>{{cite web|last=Breslau|first=Rod|url=http://www.ongamers.com/articles/nba-s-jeremy-lin-dota-2-is-more-than-just-a-game/1100-1143|title=NBA's Jeremy Lin: "Dota 2 is more than just a game"|date=April 4, 2014|publisher=[[onGamers]]|access-date=April 4, 2014|archive-date=April 6, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140406154206/http://www.ongamers.com/articles/nba-s-jeremy-lin-dota-2-is-more-than-just-a-game/1100-1143|url-status=dead}}</ref> In 2016, Lin formed his own professional ''Dota 2'' team, known as [[J.Storm]].<ref>{{cite web|last1=Van Allen|first1=Eric|title=Jeremy Lin endorses new Dota 2 team VGJ|url=https://www.espn.com/esports/story/_/id/17579673/jeremy-lin-endorse-new-dota-2-team-vgj|website=ESPN|date=September 18, 2016|access-date=October 5, 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Lin |first1=Jeremy |title=Esports vs. pro sports: Jeremy Lin is betting on both |url=https://qz.com/1438337/esports-vs-pro-sports-jeremy-lin-is-betting-on-both/ |access-date=October 31, 2018 |work=[[Quartz (publication)]] |date=October 31, 2018}}</ref>
